newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia's Kaunda plans talks with Mandela.
newsitem.headline: Zambia's Kaunda plans talks with Mandela.

text.p: Former Zambian president Kenneth Kaunda left for South Africa on Tuesday to brief President Nelson Mandela on his party's decision to boycott general elections set for November 18, a spokesman for Kaunda said.
"Dr Kaunda left for South Africa this morning to explain to President Mandela why we are not participating in the elections," Muhabi Lungu said in an interview.
He said Kaunda would also ask the Southern African Development Community (SADC), of which Zambia is a member, to take note of political developments in the country.
"We want them to make a serious assesment of what is going on in this country," Lungu said.

Kaunda said last week his United National Independence Party (UNIP) - the country's biggest opposition party - would boycott presidential and parliamentary elections on November 18 in protest at the way the poll is being run.
Six other opposition parties said they would join the boycott. The parties oppose new constitutional clauses that ban Kaunda and his deputy from contesting the elections.

Among other things, the clauses ban anyone who has served two terms or more as president from running again. Kaunda was president from independence in 1964 until he lost elections to Frederick Chiluba in 1991.
His deputy, Chief Inyambo Yeta, is disqualified by a clause banning traditional rulers from active politics.
Since Kaunda declared his boycott of the election, his party has been collecting voter cards from supporters to ensure that they do not vote.
UNIP central committee member Rabbison Chongo said the party had collected some 4,000 cards in the capital since Sunday.
President Chiluba's government says the action is illegal and has directed the state-run broadcaster to reject UNIP advertisements calling for an election boycott.
A spokesman for South Africa's department of foreign affairs said he was not aware of Kaunda's presence in the country.
